steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proving with SAT solving that every set of 30 points in general position contains an empty hexagon. Give the history of the happy ending problem and of k-holes, state our main results, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Origins: Klein's result, Erdős–Szekeres and g(k), the happy ending problem
- Computing small values of g(k), and SAT
- k-holes and h(k)
- What was known about h(6)
- Our main theorem and related results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Origins
  - 1932, Esther Klein: any 5 points in general position (no three collinear) contain 4 in convex position
  - Erdős and Szekeres (cite): for every k a smallest g(k) such that g(k) points in general position contain a k-gon (k points forming convex polygon vertices)
  - led to marriage of Szekeres and Klein -> Erdős: "happy ending problem"
  - witnesses g(k)>2^{k-2} (cite), conjectured maximal; best upper bound g(k)\leq 2^{k+o(k)} (cite)
- Small values
  - g(5)=9 needs more involved case distinction than g(4)=5 (cite)
  - g(6)=17 only in 2006: exhaustive computer search by Szekeres and Peters (cite), 1500 CPU hours
  - Marić (cite), Scheucher (cite) independently via SAT, a few CPU hours; later 10 CPU minutes (cite)
  - our approach: 8.53 CPU seconds -> SAT effective vs original method
- k-holes
  - Erdős: does every large enough point set contain a k-hole (k-gon with no point inside)?
  - h(k): smallest integer, if it exists, such that h(k) points contain a k-hole
  - h(3)=3, h(4)=5 easy (Fig. 1), coincide with original setting
  - Horton (cite): arbitrarily large sets without 7-holes
- h(6)
  - Harborth (cite), 1978: h(5)=10
  - 6-holes open until late 2000s: Gerken (cite) and Nicolás (cite) independently, h(6) finite
  - Gerken: every 9-gon yields a 6-hole -> h(6)\leq g(9)\leq 1717 (cite)
  - lower bound h(6)\geq 30: 29 points without 6-holes, Overmars (cite), local search, Figure 8
- Results
  - close the gap, answer Erdős: every 30 points yield a 6-hole -> h(6)=30
  - stronger: bounds coincide with those for counterclockwise systems (cite)
  - SAT success like Schur Number Five (cite), Keller's Conjecture (cite)
  - 6-holes + 7-gons: every 24 points contain a 6-hole or a 7-gon
- Contributions
  - compact SAT encoding, O(n^{4}) clauses vs O(n^{k})
  - partitioning with linear-time speedups on thousands of cores
  - validating SAT results by checking the proof while solving, less overhead
  - clausal proof checking for most results

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In 1932, Esther Klein showed that every set of five points in the plane in general position (meaning no three points are on a common line) has a subset of four points in convex position. Soon after, Erdős and Szekeres generalized this result. They showed that for every integer k there is a smallest integer g(k) such that every set of g(k) points in the plane in general position contains a k -gon (a subset of k points that are the vertices of a convex polygon). Because this research led to Szekeres and Klein getting married, Erdős named it the happy ending problem. Erdős and Szekeres constructed witnesses of g(k)>2^{k-2}, and they conjectured that this is maximal. The best upper bound is g(k)\leq 2^{k+o(k)}.

To determine the value g(5)=9 you need a more involved case distinction than for g(4)=5. It took until 2006 to determine g(6)=17, which was done with an exhaustive computer search by Szekeres and Peters that used 1500 CPU hours. Marić and Scheucher independently verified g(6)=17 with satisfiability (SAT) solving in a few CPU hours. Later this was reduced to 10 CPU minutes. The approach in this paper computes it in 8.53 CPU seconds, which shows how effective SAT is compared to the original method.

Erdős also asked if every sufficiently large point set contains a k -hole, which is a k -gon without a point inside. We write h(k) for the smallest integer, if it exists, such that every set of h(k) points in general position in the plane contains a k -hole. Both h(3)=3 and h(4)=5 are easy to compute (Fig. 1 illustrates this) and they are the same as in the original setting. But the answer can be very different, since Horton constructed arbitrarily large point sets that have no 7-holes.

- h(6)
  - Harborth, 1978: h(5)=10
  - 6-holes open until late 2000s; Gerken and Nicolás independently: h(6) finite
  - Gerken: every 9-gon yields a 6-hole -> h(6)\leq g(9)\leq 1717
  - lower bound h(6)\geq 30: 29 points without 6-holes, Overmars, local search, Figure 8
- Results
  - every 30 points yield a 6-hole: h(6)=30.
  - bounds coincide with counterclockwise systems; SAT success like Schur Number Five, Keller's Conjecture
  - every 24 points contain a 6-hole or a 7-gon
- Contributions
  - SAT encoding with O(n^{4}) clauses vs O(n^{k})
  - partitioning, linear-time speedups on thousands of cores
  - checking the proof while solving, less overhead
  - clausal proof checking for most results

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In 1932, Esther Klein showed that every set of five points in the plane in general position (meaning no three points are on a common line) has a subset of four points in convex position. Soon after, Erdős and Szekeres generalized this result. They showed that for every integer k there is a smallest integer g(k) such that every set of g(k) points in the plane in general position contains a k -gon (a subset of k points that are the vertices of a convex polygon). Because this research led to Szekeres and Klein getting married, Erdős named it the happy ending problem. Erdős and Szekeres constructed witnesses of g(k)>2^{k-2}, and they conjectured that this is maximal. The best upper bound is g(k)\leq 2^{k+o(k)}.

To determine the value g(5)=9 you need a more involved case distinction than for g(4)=5. It took until 2006 to determine g(6)=17, which was done with an exhaustive computer search by Szekeres and Peters that used 1500 CPU hours. Marić and Scheucher independently verified g(6)=17 with satisfiability (SAT) solving in a few CPU hours. Later this was reduced to 10 CPU minutes. The approach in this paper computes it in 8.53 CPU seconds, which shows how effective SAT is compared to the original method.

Erdős also asked if every sufficiently large point set contains a k -hole, which is a k -gon without a point inside. We write h(k) for the smallest integer, if it exists, such that every set of h(k) points in general position in the plane contains a k -hole. Both h(3)=3 and h(4)=5 are easy to compute (Fig. 1 illustrates this) and they are the same as in the original setting. But the answer can be very different, since Horton constructed arbitrarily large point sets that have no 7-holes.

Harborth showed in 1978 that h(5)=10, but whether 6 -holes exist was open until the late 2000s, when Gerken and Nicolás independently proved that h(6) is finite. Gerken proved that every 9 -gon yields a 6 -hole, and this shows that h(6)\leq g(9)\leq 1717. The best-known lower bound is h(6)\geq 30, which is witnessed by a set of 29 points without 6 -holes that Overmars found with a local search approach, see Figure 8.

We close the gap between the upper bound and the lower bound and finally answer Erdős’ question. We prove that every set of 30 points yields a 6-hole.

h(6)=30.

Our result is actually stronger. It shows that the bounds for 6 -holes in point sets are the same as the bounds for 6 -holes in counterclockwise systems. This is another success of using SAT to solve long-standing open problems in mathematics, like the results on Schur Number Five and Keller’s Conjecture.

We also look at the combination of 6 -holes and 7 -gons and show

Every set of 24 points in the plane in general position contains a 6 -hole or a 7 -gon.

We get these results through the following contributions:

- We develop a compact and effective SAT encoding for k -gon and k -hole problems that uses O(n^{4}) clauses, while existing encodings use O(n^{k}) clauses.

- We construct a partitioning of k -gon and k -hole problems that lets us solve them with linear-time speedups even when we use thousands of cores.

- We present a new method of validating SAT-solving results that checks the proof while solving the problem, with a lot less overhead.

- We verify most of the results in this paper using clausal proof checking.

steps.text:
In 1932, Esther Klein showed that every set of five points in the plane in general position (i.e., no three points on a common line) has a subset of four points in convex position. Shortly after, Erdős and Szekeres [1] generalized this result by showing that, for every integer k, there exists a smallest integer g(k) such that every set of g(k) points in the plane in general position contains a k -gon (i.e., a subset of k points forming the vertices of a convex polygon). As the research led to the marriage of Szekeres and Klein, Erdős named it the happy ending problem. Erdős and Szekeres constructed witnesses of g(k)>2^{k-2} [2], which they conjectured to be maximal. The best upper bound is g(k)\leq 2^{k+o(k)} [3,4].

Determining g(5)=9 requires a more involved case distinction than g(4)=5 [5]. It took until 2006 to determine that g(6)=17, via an exhaustive computer search by Szekeres and Peters [6] using 1500 CPU hours. Marić [7] and Scheucher [8] independently verified g(6)=17 using satisfiability (SAT) solving in a few CPU hours, which was later reduced to 10 CPU minutes [9]. The approach presented in this paper computes it in 8.53 CPU seconds, showing the effectiveness of SAT compared to the original method.

Erdős also asked whether every sufficiently large point set contains a k -hole: a k -gon without a point inside. We denote by h(k) the smallest integer—if it exists—such that every set of h(k) points in general position in the plane contains a k -hole. Both h(3)=3 and h(4)=5 are easy to compute (see Fig. 1 for an illustration) and coincide with the original setting. Yet the answer can differ considerably, as Horton [10] constructed arbitrarily large point sets without 7-holes.

While Harborth [11] showed in 1978 that h(5)=10, the existence of 6 -holes remained open until the late 2000s, when Gerken [12] and Nicolás [13] independently proved that h(6) is finite. Gerken proved that every 9 -gon yields a 6 -hole, thereby showing that h(6)\leq g(9)\leq 1717 [14]. The best-known lower bound h(6)\geq 30 is witnessed by a set of 29 points without 6 -holes, found by Overmars [15] using a local search approach, see Figure 8.

We close the gap between the upper and lower bound and answer Erdős’ question by proving that every set of 30 points yields a 6-hole.

h(6)=30.

Our result is in fact stronger and shows that the bounds for 6 -holes in point sets coincide with those for 6 -holes in counterclockwise systems [16]. This is another success of solving long-standing open problems in mathematics using SAT, similar to the results on Schur Number Five [17] and Keller’s Conjecture [18].

We also investigate the combination of 6 -holes and 7 -gons and show

Every set of 24 points in the plane in general position contains a 6 -hole or a 7 -gon.

We achieve these results through the following contributions:

- We develop a compact and effective SAT encoding for k -gon and k -hole problems that uses O(n^{4}) clauses, whereas existing encodings use O(n^{k}) clauses.

- We construct a partitioning of k -gon and k -hole problems that allows us to solve them with linear-time speedups even on thousands of cores.

- We present a novel method of validating SAT-solving results that checks the proof while solving the problem, with substantially less overhead.

- We verify most of the presented results using clausal proof checking.
